subtopic: Facing a natural disaster at home
passage:
I'm Trisha, and I used to think a flood was something each house faced alone. The week the river came into our lane, I learned otherwise.
Mridul, two doors down, has a fishing boat, and on the first evening he knocked on doors with two grown sons and life jackets for everyone. We shared his boat with turns, always two adults on board. Old Mrs Pillai was carried out first. Someone lit a big stove on the school terrace and we boiled water in huge pots all night.
By morning we had a list of who needed what, and Mridul walked it to the ward office. They sent a supply boat within hours.
One house could not have done any of that.

qa.q: Who owns the boat the neighbours shared?
What was Trisha probably feeling by the end of the week?
qa.a: Trisha felt grateful and a little humbled, having learned that a household cannot manage a flood alone.

qa.q: What could the neighbours do to be readier for a future flood?
qa.a: They could keep the group's list up to date and agree ahead of time who handles the boat, the water and the old people.

qa.q: How might Mrs Pillai have felt being carried out first?
qa.a: Mrs Pillai was probably frightened but reassured, since the neighbours put the older people ahead.

grounding: The reflection shows neighbours forming a group to share a boat, boil water, look after older people and work with the ward office.

subtopic: Facing a natural disaster at home
passage:
Ward relief desk log, day 3 of the flooding.
Sumit, a young resident of Block C, came to the desk at 8 a.m. with a handwritten sheet instead of a complaint. His building group had split the jobs overnight: two households with inflatable boats would ferry people to the main road in turns; the top-floor family with a gas cylinder would boil drinking water in big pots; four volunteers would check on the eleven elderly residents twice a day, listed by flat number. He asked us for only three things: medicines for two residents, a list of shelter spaces, and a time when their boat teams could meet our rescue team. I linked them with the fire service at noon. By evening their block had asked us for less than any other on the road.
Damini, ward volunteer

qa.q: How many elderly residents did the volunteers check on?
qa.a: The eleven elderly residents, twice a day.

qa.q: What does Sumit bringing a sheet instead of a complaint suggest about his state of mind?
qa.a: He seems calm and determined, focused on what neighbours could do together rather than on frustration with the flood.

qa.q: What else could the ward office learn from Block C?
qa.a: The office could share the block's sheet with other buildings, so each one splits boats, water and elder checks before asking for help.

qa.q: How might the elderly residents of Block C experience these days?
qa.a: Being checked twice a day, they are less likely to feel alone or forgotten while the water is high.

grounding: It shows neighbours sharing boats, boiled water and elder care and coordinating with the ward office, covering what one household could not.

subtopic: Facing a natural disaster at home
passage:
Friday, day four of the water.
Tonight I finally feel useful. This morning I sat on our roof feeling helpless, just watching the brown water. Then Bhupen-da from the corner house shouted across: 'Tenzin, you have a big pressure cooker?' Within an hour our lane had a plan scratched on the back of a calendar. Bhupen-da's fishing boat does the grocery and medicine run twice a day. Our house boils the drinking water, because we still have gas. The Lamas take turns sitting with old Mrs Rai, who can't climb stairs. At noon I rode in Bhupen-da's boat to the ward councillor's office and handed over our list. They sent purification tablets and two more boats by four. Alone we'd have been stuck. Together it almost felt organised.
Tenzin

qa.q: Who takes turns sitting with old Mrs Rai?
qa.a: The Lamas take turns sitting with old Mrs Rai.

qa.q: How did Tenzin's feelings change from morning to night?
qa.a: Tenzin moved from feeling helpless on the roof to feeling useful and hopeful once the lane shared out the work.

qa.q: What could the lane do before the next monsoon to make this faster?
qa.a: They could keep the calendar list of who has a boat, gas or spare space and share it with the ward office in advance.

qa.q: How might Mrs Rai see the lane's plan?
qa.a: Mrs Rai, who can't climb stairs, probably feels safer and less alone with neighbours taking turns to sit with her.

grounding: It shows neighbours sharing a boat, boiled water and elder care and working with the ward office, covering what one household could not.
